newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. proposes U.N. ban on anti-personnel mines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes U.N. ban on anti-personnel mines.

text.p: United States U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright introduced a resolution on Monday calling for an international agreement to ban the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel landmines.

"Such an agreement would be a great gift to the future," she said, noting an estimated 110 million such mines were scattered across more than 70 countries and saying they would claim another 100,000 victims -- mostly civilians and many of them children -- between now and the start of the new century.
"At the current rate, even if no more anti-personnel landmines are deployed, before the mines now in place are cleared the new century will be over -- and so will the six centuries following that."
While last year about 150,000 old anti-personnel mines were cleared, about two million new ones were put in place, she told the General Assembly's disarmament and international security committee.

Albright said the resolution was cosponsored by more than 70 countries and that she was acting at the direction of President Bill Clinton, who raised the issue of anti-personnel mines in speeches to the General Assembly this year and last.

The problem was not that they were exceptionally destructive but that they were prone to misuse by the desperate, the financially hard-pressed, the poorly trained and the cowardly. They were also cheap and easy to lay.

Albright said the draft called for voluntary adoption of bans on their transfer, use, production or stockpiling. She noted that many countries, including the United States, had already taken such steps.

Recognising that some governments had security concerns regarding borders or demilitarized zones, she said the United States also had such a concern. "But this should not prevent us from negotiating an agreement to end the use of anti-personnel landmines," she said.
China told the committee last month it opposed a total ban on anti-personnel mines since they were an effective means of self-defence and cited their use against Japan in the 1930s.
